bodies.intuition: A trained weight does not need sixteen bits to be useful. Quantization stores weights in four or eight, which shrinks the model enough to fit on smaller hardware and — because decoding is bottlenecked on reading weights, not on arithmetic — usually makes it faster too. The loss in quality is far smaller than the loss in precision suggests.
bodies.engineer: Map each weight group to a low-bit integer with a scale, and dequantise on the fly. Post-training quantization needs no retraining and is what most deployments use. The difficulty is outliers: a few activation channels are orders of magnitude larger than the rest, and a naive scale spends its whole range on them and flattens everything else to zero.
bodies.math: For a group with scale s = max|w|/(2^{b−1} − 1), store round(w/s) and reconstruct as s·round(w/s). Error per weight is bounded by s/2, so it falls with the group size and rises with the group's largest magnitude — which is why outlier handling, not bit width alone, decides whether a scheme survives.
